$comment: Cross-client test vectors for src/core/rules/astro/. Required by ADR 003 section 4: this maths is written once and reimplemented in Swift later, and the two implementations are policed by this file rather than by trust. Every expected value below is sourced from an outside authority and cited. None of it was generated by the TypeScript implementation it tests - a vector file produced by the code it checks proves nothing.

sources.name: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department - Sun and Moon Data for One Day
sources.precision: Published to the whole minute. A vector value is therefore the START of the minute the USNO printed, and the true event may be up to 60 seconds later. The tolerances below are sized for that.

sources.name: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department - Phases of the Moon

toleranceRationale: These are contract tolerances for any client, not a description of this implementation. They are sized as: the USNO's own minute rounding, plus room for a different-but-adequate algorithm. For reference, the TypeScript implementation measured against 108 USNO location-days spanning 1905 to 2050 and latitudes to 69.6 degrees agrees to within 34 seconds worst case, of which up to 30 seconds is the USNO's rounding - so under 4 seconds of genuine disagreement. Moon illumination agrees to 0.0034 worst case over the USNO phase tables for 2000, 2026 and 2050, and moon age to 0.021 days. If a client only just squeaks inside these tolerances, something is wrong with it.
accuracyNotes: Event times degrade above roughly 65 degrees of latitude, where the sun meets the horizon at a shallow angle and a small altitude error becomes a large time error. Whether an event happens at all stays reliable, which is the part a shaded chart depends on.

The -0.833 degree sunrise threshold is a convention covering mean refraction plus the solar semidiameter. Real refraction varies with air temperature and pressure; on a cold, high-pressure morning the observed sunrise can be a minute or two off any calculation, including the USNO's.
Observer elevation is ignored. Sea level is the right assumption for a fishing app.

conventions.localDay: sunEventsFor returns the events of the LOCAL MEAN SOLAR DAY containing 'at' - the day bounded by local solar midnight at that longitude. core/ has no timezone database, so there is no civil calendar date here. Several vectors below have events whose UTC calendar date differs from the day they belong to; that is deliberate.
conventions.phaseNames: The eight moon phase names are equal 45-degree eighths of the lunation angle, each quarter name centred on its true instant. This is an arbitrary widening of four instants into four windows, chosen so every moment has a name. It calls the moon 'full' for about 3.7 days. Note that the USNO uses the opposite convention - it reserves the four words for the instant and says 'waxing crescent' at 46% lit - so the 'name' expectations below test OUR convention and are not USNO values. Illumination is the honest number and the UI must show it beside the name.
conventions.ageDays: Days elapsed since the actual preceding new moon. Real lunations run 29.27 to 29.83 days, so this can read slightly above the 29.53-day mean. It is not clamped.

sunEvents.note: Longest day of 2026 at the station this app ships a tide fixture for. Sunset and dusk fall after midnight UTC, on 2026-06-22, while still belonging to the local solar day of 21 June - which is exactly the trap a UTC engine has to get right.
The Saturday before US daylight saving time begins. Sunrise is 11:10 UTC, which is 06:10 on the local clock (EST, UTC-5).

The Sunday US daylight saving time begins (02:00 EST becomes 03:00 EDT). Sunrise is 11:09 UTC, one minute EARLIER than the day before in UTC, but 07:09 on the local clock - an hour LATER than yesterday's 06:10. The engine must produce the UTC number; only the display layer knows about the hour jump.
The Monday after the change. UTC sunrise continues to move two minutes a day with no discontinuity whatsoever, which is the point.
A century in the past. Fixes the lower end of the date range the implementation claims to be valid over.
A quarter century in the future. Fixes the upper end of the claimed date range.

On the equator at an equinox: twelve hours of day and the fastest twilight on Earth, 21 minutes from sunset to the end of civil twilight. This is the case that sets how finely daylightSpans has to scan.

Southern hemisphere, winter, and 147 degrees east - so the local solar day begins mid-afternoon UTC on the previous calendar date. Dawn and sunrise here carry a 30 June UTC stamp and sunset carries a 1 July one, and they belong to the same local day.

Inside the Arctic Circle in midwinter: the USNO publishes 'Object continuously below the Horizon', so there is no sunrise and no sunset. There IS civil twilight around midday. sunrise and sunset must be null - a plausible-looking timestamp here would be a lie the UI cannot detect. The USNO publishes no upper transit for this day, so solarNoon is not asserted.
The same place six months later: 'Object continuously above the Horizon' and above the twilight limit. All four horizon events are null and only solar noon exists.

Far enough north that the sun stays below the civil twilight limit too: 'continuously below the Horizon' AND 'continuously below the Twilight Limit'. All four events null, and daylightSpans must return one unbroken night. No upper transit published, so solarNoon is not asserted.

daylightSpans.note: Three whole days spanning the start of US daylight saving time. Thirteen spans, every boundary a published USNO event, no gaps and no overlaps. The clock change is invisible here because the engine has no local clock to change - that is what this vector proves.
One local solar day on the equator. The two twilight spans are 21 minutes each, the shortest that occur anywhere, so this is the vector that would fail first if the scan step were made coarser.
Polar night with a twilight window: night, then a few hours of civil twilight around midday, then night again. No 'day' span at all.

Three days of midnight sun. One single 'day' span covering the entire range - the degenerate case a per-day stitching implementation gets wrong. USNO reports 'Object continuously above the Horizon' for 21, 22 and 23 June.
Three days of true polar night. One single 'night' span. USNO reports 'continuously below the Twilight Limit' for 1, 2 and 3 January.

moonPhase.note: USNO tabulated New Moon. Illumination at this instant is definitional rather than measured: at the moment the USNO tabulates, the geocentric illuminated fraction is 0 at new, 0.5 at a quarter and 1 at full, to within a few thousandths contributed by the moon's ecliptic latitude. The tolerance absorbs that.

USNO tabulated First Quarter. Illumination at this instant is definitional rather than measured: at the moment the USNO tabulates, the geocentric illuminated fraction is 0 at new, 0.5 at a quarter and 1 at full, to within a few thousandths contributed by the moon's ecliptic latitude. The tolerance absorbs that.

Illumination at this instant is definitional rather than measured: at the moment the USNO tabulates, the geocentric illuminated fraction is 0 at new, 0.5 at a quarter and 1 at full, to within a few thousandths contributed by the moon's ecliptic latitude. The tolerance absorbs that.

Illumination at this instant is definitional rather than measured: at the moment the USNO tabulates, the geocentric illuminated fraction is 0 at new, 0.5 at a quarter and 1 at full, to within a few thousandths contributed by the moon's ecliptic latitude. The tolerance absorbs that.

USNO tabulated New Moon, 26 years back. Illumination at this instant is definitional rather than measured: at the moment the USNO tabulates, the geocentric illuminated fraction is 0 at new, 0.5 at a quarter and 1 at full, to within a few thousandths contributed by the moon's ecliptic latitude. The tolerance absorbs that.

USNO tabulated Full Moon, 24 years forward. Illumination at this instant is definitional rather than measured: at the moment the USNO tabulates, the geocentric illuminated fraction is 0 at new, 0.5 at a quarter and 1 at full, to within a few thousandths contributed by the moon's ecliptic latitude. The tolerance absorbs that.
Exactly 3.000 days after the USNO New Moon of 2026-03-19 01:23 UTC, so the age must read 3.000 days. The expected age comes from the USNO instant, not from this implementation.
Exactly 14.000 days after the USNO New Moon of 2026-06-15 02:54 UTC. Lands about a day short of the full moon of 29 June 23:56, because this lunation runs longer than the 29.53-day mean.
Exactly 29.000 days after the USNO New Moon of 2026-01-18 19:52 UTC, one day before the next new moon at 2026-02-17 12:01. Guards the wrap at the end of a lunation.
